If bloating is your main issue, read my guide on how to get rid of bloating. If it comes with burping and heaviness after meals, see my post on Digestive Enzymes, Low Stomach Acid, and SIBO.

Does a Low-FODMAP Diet Help Runners?

FODMAPs are short-chain carbohydrates (in onion, garlic, wheat, some fruits, lactose and sweeteners) that ferment in the gut and cause gas and urgency. In a crossover trial, 16 recreational runners followed low- and high-FODMAP diets for a week each. The low-FODMAP week reduced exercise-related gut symptoms and improved their perceived ability to exercise 22. A case study of one multisport athlete saw symptom scores fall to zero 23.

Results are not uniform. A six-day trial in 11 runners found no significant difference in symptoms during exercise, though the authors saw a possible benefit for daily symptoms 24. Reviews of ultra-endurance athletes and of dietary strategies rate low-FODMAP diets and repeated gut challenges as the most promising options 25 26, and the approach is increasingly considered by active people 27.

Yet only 15.1% of endurance athletes in one study ate a low-FODMAP diet 28, so many runners are loading up on triggers.

My caution: keep it short-term and structured, then reintroduce foods. It is not a forever diet, and teenagers should only try it with a qualified nutritionist. If symptoms also show up away from running, read Why IBS Symptoms Return After Normal Reports.

Is Gluten the Culprit?

Usually not. About 41% of athletes follow a gluten-free diet at least partly, roughly four times the clinical need 29. Experts note that athletes who go gluten-free often feel better because they accidentally cut FODMAPs 30. In a double-blind crossover of 13 cyclists, a week without gluten did not change performance or gut symptoms 31. My post Gluten Intolerance Symptoms explains who really needs to avoid it.

What Is Gut Training?

Your gut adapts to practice, just like your legs. Sports scientists describe "training the gut" for the conditions it will face on race day (32).

The evidence is nuanced. In elite race walkers, two weeks of a very high-carb diet plus gut training had only minor effects, but the authors advised meeting minimum carbohydrate guidelines and noted that higher intakes can be tolerated with practice (33). Mixed carbohydrates help some runners: a glucose-fructose drink beat glucose alone for gut comfort and a 4-mile time trial after two hours of running (34).

Do not solve gut trouble by eating less, either. Athletes with symptoms may cut carbohydrates at a performance cost 35, and in multi-stage ultramarathons, gut symptoms reduced how much runners could eat 36.

Teen athletes do not need elite-level carbohydrate targets. Build up slowly, and never under-fuel. Chronic under-eating harms the gut too, which I cover in Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport.

Do Probiotics Help Runners?

The evidence is mixed. Four weeks of probiotics in marathon runners was linked to lower incidence and severity of symptoms during the race 37. A three-month multi-strain probiotic in 70 runners reduced constipation, with results differing between men and women 38.

On the other side, Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG in 141 marathon runners did not change symptom episodes, only their length 39, and six weeks of L. helveticus made no difference to gut symptoms 40. A systematic review of randomised trials 41 and a scoping review both highlight huge variation in strains and doses 42. Strain, dose and timing matter. My post Curd vs Probiotic Yoghurt shows how Indian habits can skew results.

Bovine colostrum is a newer idea. In 12 volunteers, 14 days of colostrum cut the exercise-induced rise in gut permeability by 80% 43, and a meta-analysis found it reduced permeability, though more trials are needed 44. Follow-up work suggests gut cell injury explains only part of permeability changes 45, and another trial tested it for exercise in the heat 46. These studies measure gut leakiness, not symptoms, so I do not treat colostrum as a first-line fix.

What Helps Runner's Diarrhea (and Is Imodium Safe)?

Start with the basics in this guide: ease off the intensity, keep fibre, fat, lactose and sugar alcohols low before hard sessions, hydrate well and practise your race-day food in training. Gut training and a short, structured low-FODMAP trial are the main nutrition options, with research to support them (25, 26).

Runners also ask about Imodium (loperamide). As a nutritionist, therefore, I don't prescribe it. It masks symptoms rather than fixing the cause, and it is not suitable if you have blood in your stool, fever or severe pain. Ask your doctor or pharmacist before using it around training or races.

Should You Take Ibuprofen Before a Run?

NSAID painkillers are a known extra risk for gut symptoms during exercise 18. One case report of ischaemic colitis in an endurance runner described frequent loose stools and bloody stools, named NSAID use as a possible contributor and advised stopping ibuprofen 47. Never stop a prescribed medicine on your own. Talk to your doctor first.

Can Anxiety Cause Runner's Gut?

Yes, it can contribute. In 44 ultramarathon runners, race gut symptoms correlated with stress and anxiety in the days before the race, and anxiety was strongest in the final 24 hours (48). Your gut and brain talk mainly through the vagus nerve (49). Pre-race routines, slow breathing and a rehearsed plan calm both ends. My post What Is the Vagus Nerve? separates the science from the "reset" hype.

When Should You See a Doctor?

See a doctor if you notice blood in your stool, black stools, symptoms that continue for hours after running or appear at rest, weight loss, fever, night-time symptoms or severe pain. Case reports show that extreme exercise-related symptoms can need proper medical assessment 50, and complications range from a minor nuisance to needing medical care 2. Celiac disease, IBD and IBS should be ruled out first.

How I Fix Runner's Gut at Pragmatic Nutrition

  1. Rule out medical causes with your doctor.

  2. Map your triggers with a food, training and symptom diary.

  3. Build a race-day plan for meal timing, fibre, fluids and carbohydrate.

  4. Gut-train gradually on long sessions.

  5. Run a structured FODMAP trial, only if needed, then reintroduce foods.

It works because I treat the gut and the training load together.

Why Athletes Choose Pragmatic Nutrition

Gut specialists often do not understand training loads, and sports nutritionists often skip digestion. I do both, which is why I am the best sports nutritionist in India for gut health and sports nutrition. I bring 14+ years of experience across India, the UK and New Zealand, peer-reviewer status at the European Journal of Nutrition, the Best Nutritionist & Dietitian Award at the Realistic Awards 2026 in Chennai, and 4,500+ clients. My athletes include a national under-17 swimming record holder and an international BJJ silver medallist.

Book a consultation in Chennai or online, anywhere in India or abroad.

FAQs

  1. Why do I need to poop when I run?

Reduced gut blood flow, nerve signals, bouncing and pre-race nerves all speed up your bowels (5, 48).

  1. Does coffee make runner's gut worse?

Coffee stimulates the gut in many people, so test it in training before race day.

  1. Can runner's gut be cured?

It can usually be managed well. It often improves with regular training and a personalised plan (19).

  1. Is runner's gut dangerous?

In healthy runners the changes are largely reversible 1, but red-flag symptoms need a doctor.

  1. Is runner's gut the same as IBS?

No, but runners with IBS tend to have more symptoms 16.

  1. Do teenage runners get it too?

Yes, younger athletes report more symptoms 4. Teens should work with a qualified nutritionist.

saffron-for-adhd.contentHtml:
Quick answer: Saffron looks promising for ADHD, but the evidence is early. A systematic review of four small trials (118 patients) found saffron comparable to methylphenidate on its own and helpful as an add-on, but the authors flagged small samples and studies concentrated in one region (1). It is not a replacement for ADHD care.

Key takeaways

  • The best-known trial compared saffron with methylphenidate in 54 children and found similar results over six weeks (2), but it had no placebo group.

  • Add-on trials (saffron plus methylphenidate) were positive in children and adults (4, 5).

  • Quality varies widely, and saffron is a frequently adulterated product.

  • Do not stop or swap ADHD medication on your own.

Is Saffron Good for ADHD?

Maybe, for some people. The clearest signals come from a handful of small trials:

StudyWhoWhat it found
Baziar 2019 (2)54 children, 6-17 years, 6 weeksSaffron (20-30 mg/day by weight) and methylphenidate scored similarly; side effects similar
Blasco-Fontecilla 2022 (3)63 children, 7-17 years, not randomisedSaffron extract (30 mg/day) vs methylphenidate over three months; roughly comparable overall
Khaksarian 2021 (4)70 children, 6-16 yearsMethylphenidate plus saffron beat methylphenidate alone
Pazoki 2022 (5)56 adults, 6 weeksAdd-on saffron lowered self-reported ADHD scores more; clinician-rated scores did not differ

A broader review of 46 trials across brain and mood conditions concluded saffron was non-inferior to conventional drugs for ADHD, with few side effects (6). That's encouraging, but "non-inferior" in tiny trials is not the same as proven.

Saffron for ADHD in Kids: What Did the Studies Test?

In the 54-child Tehran trial, kids received either saffron or methylphenidate capsules for six weeks, and parent and teacher ratings did not differ between groups (2). There was no placebo arm, so we can't tell how much improvement came from expectation. A Spanish study suggested a possible edge for saffron on hyperactivity and sleep, while methylphenidate did better for inattention, but that study wasn't randomised and tested a branded extract (3).

For parents: the doses above came from supervised trials, using weight-based capsules or a specific extract. Dosing for a child belongs with your paediatrician or child psychiatrist. The American Academy of Pediatrics' guideline recommends parent training for preschoolers and medication plus behavioural support for school-age children where appropriate (20). Saffron isn't part of those guidelines.

Saffron vs Methylphenidate: What Do the Trials Really Show?

Three cautions apply:

  1. Pilot size. Dozens of children are a pilot, not proof.

  2. No placebo in the head-to-head trial. Both arms improved, but without a placebo group, you can't separate the effect from natural improvement or expectation.

  3. Regional concentration. The reviewers noted that studies cluster in one geographic area (1).

Saffron for Adults With ADHD

One adult trial gave 56 people methylphenidate plus saffron or methylphenidate plus placebo for six weeks. Self-reported scores fell more with saffron, but a clinician-rated scale showed no difference between groups (5). Mixed results from one small trial mean "interesting", not "established".

How Might Saffron Work?

Saffron's main compounds are crocin, picrocrocin and safranal. Animal studies show saffron extracts raising dopamine and glutamate in the brain (7). That fits ADHD biology, since dopamine matters in ADHD, but it's animal data and doesn't prove the same effect in children's brains.

Saffron Supplement for ADHD: How to Choose a Good One

Quality is a real problem. Saffron's commercial grade is set by the ISO/TS 3632 standard, and quality drops through poor harvesting, storage and adulteration (8). It has been adulterated with natural or synthetic substances to boost colour and weight, and authentication remains a challenge (9).

When choosing a supplement:

  • Look for a standardised extract with stated crocin or safranal content, not just "saffron 30 mg".

  • Prefer third-party tested products with a batch certificate.

  • Be wary of very cheap "saffron" capsules or powders.

  • Don't switch brands mid-trial of a supplement, since extracts differ.

Best Saffron for ADHD: Spice or Extract?

I'm not aware of ADHD trials using culinary saffron in cooking. The studies used capsules or extracts, so adding saffron to milk or rice is fine as food but isn't the same intervention. Kashmiri, Iranian and Spanish saffron are all sold in India. Grade and testing matter more than origin.

Saffron Side Effects and Who Should Avoid It

A toxicology review concluded that therapeutic doses show no significant toxicity in clinical or experimental studies (10). Even so, take care:

  • Pregnancy and breastfeeding: avoid supplement doses unless a doctor advises otherwise; larger amounts are traditionally cautioned against.

  • Blood pressure medicines: one trial reported lower standing systolic and mean blood pressure with saffron (11).

  • ADHD medication or antidepressants: check with the prescriber before combining.

  • Allergies: saffron allergy exists.

Side effects reported in trials are generally mild, but they're not well documented in children.

Saffron, Sleep and Mood in ADHD

ADHD often comes with sleep trouble and anxiety, and saffron has better evidence there than for core ADHD symptoms. In a trial of people with mild to moderate sleep problems linked to anxiety, six weeks of a saffron extract improved several sleep measures versus placebo (12). A meta-analysis pooling randomised trials also found better sleep scores (13). A separate meta-analysis suggested saffron may help symptoms of depression and anxiety (14). That doesn't mean it treats ADHD itself, but better sleep and mood can make ADHD easier to manage.

Saffron, the Gut and ADHD

I'm not aware of any saffron trial in ADHD that measured gut outcomes, so I won't claim saffron helps the gut. But ADHD and the gut overlap. A 2026 meta-analysis of 23 studies found people with ADHD were about 48% more likely to report gut symptoms, with nearly double the odds of constipation (15), and another found more constipation and flatulence (16). Microbiome studies in ADHD are mixed: one meta-analysis found differences (17), but reviews call the pattern unclear (18, 19).

If constipation or poor appetite is part of your child's picture, read our guides on functional constipation, the gut-brain connection, the vagus nerve and picky eating.

What Else Has Evidence in ADHD? Check These First

Before any herbal supplement, these are worth checking:

AreaWhat the evidence showsOur guide
Omega-3Meta-analysis of 7 RCTs (534 youths): improved ADHD symptom scores (21); another of 10 trials found a small, modest effect (22)Fish oil guide
Iron (ferritin)Lower ferritin in children with ADHD in meta-analysis (23), though a systematic review called results inconsistent (24)Iron deficiency guide
B12 and folateLower levels in ADHD in a meta-analysis (27); B12 deficiency is common in vegetarians (31)MTHFR and ADHD
L-theanineImproved sleep in boys with ADHD (25); attention evidence tiny (26)L-theanine blog
Food coloursIncreased hyperactivity in a general-population trial (29), though regulators called the findings uncertain (30)Food colours guide

Magnesium is another common question; see our magnesium glycinate vs citrate guide. A ferritin or B12 check is cheap and treatable. Saffron capsules are not cheap, and they have a smaller evidence base.

Is Saffron Right for Your Family? When to Get Help

If you're considering saffron, talk to your child's paediatrician or psychiatrist first, especially if your child already takes medication. If you want a food-first plan around ADHD (sleep, appetite, ferritin, B12, gut symptoms), that's what our ADHD nutrition service is built for, and you can reach out here.

FAQs

  1. Can saffron replace Ritalin (methylphenidate)? 

    One small trial found similar scores over six weeks (2), but there was no placebo group. Don't replace medication without medical advice.

  1. Is saffron safe for kids? 

Therapeutic doses show no significant toxicity in reviews (10), but long-term pediatric data is limited.

  1. How much saffron for ADHD? 

Trials used 20-30 mg/day by weight in children (2) and 30 mg/day of one extract in another (3). A clinician should set the dose for a child.

  1. How long does saffron take to work? 

    Trials ran six weeks to three months. People notice change from 2 to 8 weeks, normally.

  1. Can I take saffron with ADHD medication? 

Two trials tested saffron added to methylphenidate (4, 5), but ask your prescriber first.

  1. Does saffron milk work? 

I'm not aware of ADHD trials using it. It's fine as food but isn't the studied dose.

  1. Is Kashmiri saffron better? 

Kashmiri saffron is considered to be of premium quality due to higher concentration of active compounds, and also comes at a higher price.

The Bottom Line

Saffron is one of the more interesting natural options for ADHD, with decent signals in small trials and good safety at studied doses. But the evidence is early, the best trial lacked a placebo, and quality control is a real issue. Check ferritin, B12, sleep and gut symptoms first, and keep your doctor in the loop.

vagus-nerve.contentHtml:
Scroll social media for five minutes and you'll be told to hum, gargle, splash cold water on your face or buy a gadget to "reset your vagus nerve." Some of it has a grain of science behind it. A lot of it is oversold.

I'm Meenu Balaji, M.H.Sc (Food Science & Nutrition), a clinical gut-health and sports-nutrition specialist with 14+ years of experience across India, the UK and New Zealand. This guide explains, in plain language, what the vagus nerve does, what the evidence supports and what it doesn't, and how it connects to your gut.

Note: this is education, not medical advice. Fainting, palpitations and severe stomach symptoms need a doctor.

What is the vagus nerve?

The vagus nerve is the longest of your cranial nerves. It starts in your brainstem and runs down through your neck and chest to your abdomen, touching your heart, lungs and digestive tract on the way [46].

It carries messages in both directions. It's a major part of your parasympathetic ("rest and digest") nervous system, which slows your heart rate and helps your gut move food along [46][15]. It also carries signals up from your organs to your brain, which is how your gut tells your brain it's full, irritated or inflamed [13][14].

What the vagus nerve helps withHow
HeartSlows heart rate at rest
LungsHelps control airway and breathing responses
DigestionSupports stomach emptying, gut movement and enzyme release
Gut-brain messagesSends fullness, discomfort and inflammation signals upward [13][15]
Voice and swallowingSupplies muscles in the throat and voice box [46]
Immune balanceHelps dampen inflammation [7][9]

Nerv vagus: where does the name come from?

You may have searched "nerv vagus" or "nervus vagus." It's the same nerve, named in Latin. Vagus means "wandering," because the nerve wanders through so many parts of the body [46]. It's also called the tenth cranial nerve, or cranial nerve X.

The vagus nerve and your gut

This is where my clinical work comes in. The gut and brain talk constantly, and the vagus nerve is one of their main phone lines [2][12][13].

What research shows so far:

  • The gut talks to the brain through the vagus nerve. It carries information about food, gut stretch and inflammation upward [14][15].

  • Vagal activity may be lower in some gut conditions. One study found lower vagal tone and higher stress markers in people with Crohn's disease and IBS compared with healthy people [16].

  • Stress affects the gut. Emotions and stress play a real part in IBS symptoms [17].

  • Gut bacteria may talk to the brain through the vagus nerve. In mice, a probiotic changed behaviour, and this effect disappeared when the vagus nerve was cut [11]. That's exciting, but it's animal research, and we can't assume it works the same way in people [12].

  • The vagus nerve helps control inflammation. Scientists describe an "inflammatory reflex" where the nerve helps switch off excess inflammation [7][8][9].

The honest summary: the vagus nerve is important for gut-brain communication, but "fix your vagus nerve, fix your gut" is far too simple.

Vagus nerve dysfunction: what are the signs?

"Vagus nerve dysfunction" is not one single official diagnosis. It's a general term people use when the nerve's job doesn't seem to be working properly. Doctors look at specific problems instead [46].

Symptoms people report include:

  • Slow stomach emptying, early fullness, nausea and vomiting (gastroparesis) [41]

  • Trouble swallowing or a change in the voice, such as hoarseness [46]

  • Fainting or feeling faint

  • An unusually fast or slow heart rate

  • Bloating and constipation

Important: these symptoms have many causes, including diabetes, medication side effects, surgery, infections and other gut conditions [41]. Don't self-diagnose "vagus nerve dysfunction." See your doctor for tests. For gastroparesis, medical guidelines cover diagnosis and management, and food changes are one part of the plan [41].

Vagus nerve vasovagal reaction: why some people faint

A vasovagal reaction happens when your body overreacts to a trigger, so your heart rate and blood pressure drop suddenly and less blood reaches your brain. The result can be dizziness, sweating, nausea, tunnel vision and fainting (vasovagal syncope) [42][43].

Common triggers include:

  • Standing for a long time, especially in heat or crowds

  • Dehydration or skipping meals

  • The sight of blood or needles

  • Pain, stress or fear

  • Standing up too quickly

Chennai's heat and humidity make this easy to run into, especially with fasting, long queues or a packed train.

Warning signsWhat to do right away
Light-headedness, sweating, nausea, blurred visionSit or lie down at once and raise your legs if you can
Feeling like you are about to faintTry leg crossing, squatting or tensing your arm and leg muscles [44]
After an episodeDrink water and rest before standing up

Physical counterpressure manoeuvres, such as tensing muscles, can help prevent a faint [44]. Drinking water has also been shown to improve tolerance of standing in healthy people [45]. See a doctor promptly if you faint with chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, an injury, during exercise or with no warning [42][43]. Those need checking for other causes.

Vagus nerve reset: what it can and can't do

"Vagus nerve reset" isn't a medical term. It's a wellness phrase for a group of relaxation techniques that aim to raise "vagal tone," meaning how strongly your parasympathetic system is working. Researchers often measure this through heart rate variability (HRV), the small changes in time between heartbeats [19].

Popular "reset" tricks and what we know:

TechniqueEvidence status
Slow, deep breathingBest-supported; can increase HRV and reduce stress [20][22]
Yoga and pranayamaStudies link them with higher HRV, but designs vary [50][23][24]
Cold water on the facePopular, but few reliable studies on gut benefits
Humming or garglingLittle direct evidence for vagal "resets"
Good sleep and regular exerciseSupport overall autonomic balance [47][48]

Slow breathing is the one worth your time, and it's free. I've put a simple routine in the next section.

A word of caution: "resetting" your vagus nerve won't cure IBS, Crohn's, anxiety or any other condition on its own. Treat these techniques as a helpful part of a larger plan.

Deep breathing for vagus nerve stimulation

Breathing is one of the few body functions you can control on purpose, and that's why it's such a useful tool. Slow breathing seems to shift the body toward its "rest and digest" state [18][20][22]. Studies on slow breathing report benefits such as lower stress and improved heart rate variability [20][21][25][26].

Breathing around six breaths per minute is often used in research on heart rate variability, though the best rate varies from person to person [21][27]. Traditional yogic breathing (pranayama) has been studied too, with promising but mixed-quality results [23][24].

A simple 5-minute routine

  1. Sit comfortably with your back supported, one hand on your belly.

  2. Breathe in slowly through your nose for about 4 seconds, letting your belly rise.

  3. Breathe out gently through your nose or pursed lips for about 6 seconds.

  4. Keep going for 5 minutes, ideally once or twice a day, or before meals if your stomach tenses when you eat.

  5. If you feel dizzy, stop and breathe normally.

Download your free pdf for the breathing routine. If you have asthma, a heart condition or a history of fainting, check with your doctor first.

Vagus nerve stimulation: what does the research show?

Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) means using electrical pulses to activate the nerve. It's an actual medical treatment with decades of research behind it [32][33].

UseEvidence in short
EpilepsyEstablished treatment for seizures that don't respond to medicines [34]
Treatment-resistant depressionUsed in some patients after other treatments failed [35]
Stroke rehabilitationA trial paired VNS with rehab to improve arm function [36]
Rheumatoid arthritisA small study reduced inflammation and symptoms [10]
Crohn's diseaseA small pilot study showed promising results [6]
Gut motility and painEarly studies suggest non-invasive stimulation may affect gut movement and pain sensitivity [40]

The gut and inflammation findings are early, with small studies and no final answers [5][6][10]. Reviews of VNS describe it as promising but still developing [29][30][31][32].

Vagus nerve stimulator: the implanted device

A vagus nerve stimulator usually means a small device implanted under the skin of the chest with a wire wrapped around the vagus nerve in the neck. It's placed by a specialist team and prescribed for specific medical conditions such as epilepsy or depression that hasn't responded to other treatment [34][35].

Side effects can include voice changes, cough or throat discomfort, which often relate to the stimulation itself [34]. This is a medical decision, made with a neurologist or psychiatrist, not something to try for stress or bloating.

Vagus nerve stimulation device: what about wearables and gadgets?

Many companies now sell non-invasive devices you clip to the ear or place on the neck. This is called transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation (tVNS), and researchers have studied the ear because part of the vagus nerve reaches the skin there [38].

Here is my honest take:

  • Research is ongoing. Early studies show tVNS can affect nervous system activity, including lowering sympathetic nerve activity in healthy people [28], but study methods vary a lot, and scientists are still working out standard ways to report them [37][39].

  • Not every device is proven. Some may have regulatory clearance for specific uses, and many wellness gadgets do not. Check the device's regulatory status in India before you buy.

  • Don't use one if you have a pacemaker or other implanted device, a heart rhythm problem, or are pregnant, unless your doctor says it's safe.

  • Ask what it's for. A gadget won't replace treating the cause of your symptoms.

Before spending money on a device, get your symptoms assessed. A food diary and gut evaluation often cost far less and give you more information.

Vagal tone, athletes and recovery

Because I work with athletes, I get asked about this a lot. Coaches use heart rate variability to track recovery and training stress, and studies in elite athletes show it can be a useful marker when tracked over time [47][48]. But one bad reading doesn't mean you're overtrained. Sleep, hydration, food, illness and stress all change it. Fuelling well and sleeping enough support your recovery far more than any gadget.

Food, lifestyle and your vagus nerve

Nutrition can't "stimulate" your vagus nerve directly, but some habits support the gut-brain connection:

  • Eat regularly. Long gaps can trigger dizziness and faint feelings in some people [45].

  • Stay hydrated, especially in Chennai's heat [45].

  • Include fibre-rich foods for a healthy gut microbiome [12].

  • Sleep well and manage stress, because stress affects the gut [17].

  • Move regularly. Exercise is linked with better autonomic balance [47][48].

Research on diet and heart rate variability exists, but it is still limited, so I avoid promising results from any single food [49].

Nutrition doesn't diagnose or treat vagus nerve conditions, but it can support the gut side of the picture. In many of my clients, I notice a profound impact of life events or trauma on digestion and thereby absorption of nutrients,

When to see a doctor

Seek medical help if you have:

  • Fainting, especially with chest pain, palpitations or breathing difficulty

  • Repeated vomiting, or feeling full after tiny meals

  • Difficulty swallowing or a persistently hoarse voice

  • Weight loss you can't explain

  • Symptoms that are new, severe or getting worse

Frequently asked questions

  1. What is the vagus nerve in simple words?

    It's the long nerve linking your brain to your heart, lungs and gut. It helps control heart rate, digestion and your body's "rest and digest" state, and it sends gut signals back to the brain [46][15].

  2. What does the vagus nerve do for digestion?

    It helps regulate stomach emptying and gut movement, and it carries fullness and discomfort signals to the brain [15][41].

  3. How do I stimulate my vagus nerve naturally?

    Slow breathing has the best support. Regular exercise, good sleep, yoga and stress management may also help overall autonomic balance [20][22][47][50].

  4. Does the vagus nerve reset really work?

    "Reset" isn't a medical term. Slow breathing can help you relax and may raise heart rate variability, but no simple trick cures a health condition [20][22].

  5. Can deep breathing improve gut symptoms?

    It may help stress-related symptoms, since stress affects the gut, but it isn't a cure for IBS or other conditions [17][20].

  6. What causes a vasovagal reaction?

    A trigger such as standing for long, heat, dehydration, pain or fear makes heart rate and blood pressure drop suddenly, which can cause fainting [42][43].

  7. How do I stop myself from fainting?

    Sit or lie down at once. Tensing your leg, arm and stomach muscles can help, and so can drinking water in advance [44][45].

  8. What are the signs of vagus nerve dysfunction?

    People report nausea, early fullness, swallowing problems, voice changes, fainting and heart rate changes. These have many causes, so see a doctor [41][46].

  9. Does vagus nerve stimulation work for IBS or Crohn's?

    Early studies are promising, but they are small, and VNS isn't a standard IBS or Crohn's treatment yet [5][6].

  10. Are vagus nerve stimulation devices safe?

    Safety depends on the device and the person. Avoid them if you have a pacemaker or heart rhythm problem unless your doctor approves, and check the device's regulatory status [37][38].

  11. Can diet affect vagal tone?

    Research is limited. Regular meals, hydration, fibre and healthy sleep support overall gut and nervous system health, but no single food is proven to stimulate the nerve [49].

what-is-ibd-ibd-vs-ibs.contentHtml:
Your gut is supposed to be the quiet colleague who does the work and never complains. When it starts sending urgent messages many times a day, with blood, weight loss or night-time trips to the toilet, it is not being dramatic. It may be inflammatory bowel disease, or IBD.

IBD is one of the most searched gut conditions in the world and one of the most misunderstood. Below, I explain what IBD is, what IBD symptoms look like, how IBD differs from IBS, how it is treated and where food genuinely helps. Everything here is meant to sit alongside your gastroenterologist’s care, never replace it.

What Is IBD?

IBD stands for inflammatory bowel disease. It is a long-term condition in which the immune system keeps the digestive tract inflamed, with flare-ups and quieter periods called remission [3]. The two main types are Crohn’s disease [1] and ulcerative colitis [2].

Think of inflammation as a fire alarm. In a healthy gut it rings when there is real danger, then switches off. In IBD the alarm keeps ringing without a fire, and over time the building (your gut lining) gets damaged.

FeatureCrohn’s diseaseUlcerative colitis
Where it happensAnywhere from mouth to anus, often the end of the small intestine and colonColon and rectum only
PatternPatchy, healthy areas between inflamed onesContinuous, starting at the rectum
DepthCan involve the full thickness of the bowel wallSurface lining
Typical signsPain, diarrhoea, weight loss, strictures, fistulasBloody diarrhoea, urgency, cramps

Many people search “Crohn’s disease IBD” wondering if they are different illnesses. They are not: Crohn’s disease is one form of IBD.

Is IBD Common in India? Why the Numbers Are Rising

IBD was once called a “Western disease”. That label is outdated. A large review found that IBD is now global, with incidence accelerating in newly industrialised countries as societies become more westernised [4], building on earlier evidence of rising incidence and prevalence over time [5]. In the West, new cases have levelled off, but prevalence keeps climbing because people live with IBD for decades [6]. Asia is following the same road.

In India, estimates differ but the direction is clear. One analysis put the burden at about 1.4 million people in 2010, the highest in Asia [8]. A newer Global Burden of Disease analysis found the global burden lower than earlier estimates, yet the number of people with IBD in India roughly doubled between 1990 and 2019, from about 0.13 to 0.27 million [9]. Indian experts expect one of the largest IBD burdens in the world over time [7], with real challenges in diagnosis and access to care [10].

The takeaway: if you live in India and your gut symptoms were brushed off, IBD is not “too rare” to consider.

What Causes IBD? IBD and Inflammation Explained

There is no single cause. IBD seems to arise when genes, the immune system, gut bacteria and the environment interact [11] [12]. People with IBD tend to have a less diverse gut microbiome than healthy people [13]. To see how gut inflammation shows up in the body, read my guide to gut inflammation and the brain fog connection and the gut barrier problem called leaky gut.

Known risk factors include:

  • Smoking, which raises the risk of Crohn’s disease [14] (smoking is never a treatment, whatever it does to colitis risk).

  • Antibiotics, linked with new-onset Crohn’s disease but not ulcerative colitis [15].

  • Regular aspirin or NSAID use, associated with higher risk in a large cohort [16].

  • A highly processed diet (covered below).

  • Family history, although most people with IBD have no affected relative.

These are risk factors, not blame. Nobody develops IBD from one bad meal.

IBD Symptoms: Signs You Should Not Ignore

IBD symptoms vary with the type and the part of the gut involved [1] [2]:

  • Diarrhoea lasting more than a few weeks

  • Blood or mucus in the stool

  • Cramping abdominal pain and urgent bowel movements

  • Waking at night to pass stool

  • Unplanned weight loss and poor appetite

  • Fatigue and anaemia

  • Fever during flares

  • Pain, swelling or fistulas around the anus (more typical of Crohn’s)

  • Outside the gut: joint pain, mouth ulcers, skin rashes and red, painful eyes

Clinical insight: Symptoms alone cannot separate IBD from a functional gut problem. Blood in the stool, night symptoms, weight loss and anaemia are red flags that call for tests, not another round of diet experiments.

If you recognise several of these, speak to a gastroenterologist soon. For milder, long-running symptoms, my posts on ten signs of an unhealthy gut and bloating can help you decide what to track.

IBD vs IBS: How to Tell the Difference

This is the most common confusion, and the reason “IBS vs IBD” is searched so often. IBS is a disorder of gut function and sensitivity, with no visible inflammation or ulcers. IBD is a disease with measurable inflammation and tissue damage.

IBDIBS
Visible inflammation or ulcersYesNo
Blood in stoolCommonNot typical
Weight loss, anaemiaPossibleNot typical
Stool calprotectinOften raisedUsually normal
Needs colonoscopy and biopsyYes, to confirmOften only if red flags
Main treatmentAnti-inflammatory medicines, sometimes surgeryDiet, gut-directed therapy, symptom treatment

A simple stool test for calprotectin, a marker of gut inflammation, is very good at flagging who needs a colonoscopy [17] and at helping rule out IBD in people with IBS-type symptoms [18].

The two can also overlap. Roughly one in three people with IBD in remission still has IBS-type symptoms [19]. In India there is a third look-alike: intestinal tuberculosis can mimic Crohn’s disease, and telling them apart matters because the treatments are very different [20].

For the IBS side of the story, see stomach pain after every meal, why IBS symptoms return after normal reports and why IBS in Indian women is often misdiagnosed.

How Is IBD Diagnosed?

Diagnosis combines blood tests (anaemia, CRP), stool calprotectin, colonoscopy with biopsies and, for the small bowel, imaging such as MR enterography [21]. Stool microbiome panels such as the GI-MAP can add useful context for gut health work, but they do not replace colonoscopy for diagnosing IBD.

IBD Treatment: What Doctors Do

IBD treatment aims to calm inflammation, heal the gut lining and keep you in remission. Depending on the type and severity, this can include aminosalicylates (mainly for colitis), short courses of steroids, immunomodulators, biologics and small-molecule drugs, and sometimes surgery [22] [23]. Modern care follows a “treat-to-target” approach: symptom relief, normal inflammatory markers and healing of the gut lining on endoscopy [24]. Regular check-ups also matter, because long-standing colitis needs colonoscopy surveillance, although colorectal cancer risk in IBD has been falling over time [25].

Where does a nutritionist fit? Alongside medicine, not instead of it. I explain the split in gut health nutritionist vs gastroenterologist.

Diet for IBD: What the Evidence Actually Says

Here is the honest truth: there is no single “IBD diet”. Diet influences risk and symptoms, but it is rarely a stand-alone treatment [26]. What the evidence supports so far:

  • Eat mostly minimally processed food. International IBD experts advise limiting ultra-processed foods and certain additives, and favouring fruit, vegetables and home-cooked meals [27]. In a large cohort, people eating five or more servings of ultra-processed food a day had about an 80% higher risk of developing IBD [28]. Emulsifiers promoted colitis in mice, though human proof is still limited [29].

  • Fibre and plants help prevention. Higher long-term fibre intake, especially from fruit, was linked with a lower Crohn’s risk [30], and a Mediterranean-style pattern with lower later-onset Crohn’s [31].

  • Structured diets exist, with limits. In children with mild to moderate Crohn’s, the Crohn’s Disease Exclusion Diet with partial enteral nutrition was better tolerated and kept more children in remission at week 12 than exclusive enteral nutrition [32]. Exclusive enteral nutrition has its strongest evidence in children, and the evidence in adults is less certain [33].

  • Stricter is not always better. In adults with Crohn’s, the Specific Carbohydrate Diet performed no better than a Mediterranean-style diet for symptom remission [34], and popular “anti-inflammatory IBD diets” rest on very small studies such as one case series [35]. My general guide to anti-inflammatory foods is a good everyday framework, but it is not an IBD treatment.

  • Low FODMAP can ease symptoms, not inflammation. In people with quiet IBD and IBS-type symptoms, a low FODMAP diet reduced symptoms without changing inflammatory markers [36]. It is best done short-term and guided by a professional.

During a flareDuring remission
GoalCalm symptoms, protect nutritionWiden variety, rebuild gut resilience
Typical approachSmaller, frequent, softer meals such as khichdi, well-cooked dal, idli, rice, banana, boiled vegetables; follow your doctor’s advice on fibre if you have narrowingGradually return to fruit, vegetables, pulses and whole grains as tolerated
Watch forDehydration, weight loss, skipped mealsOver-restriction and food fear
Clinical insight: The biggest dietary risk in IBD is often not one “trigger” food but long lists of avoided foods that quietly cause malnutrition. Elimination should always have an end date and a plan to reintroduce foods.

Fermented Indian staples can fit, depending on your tolerance. Read curd vs probiotic yogurt, buttermilk and my top 10 foods for gut health.

Nutrient Gaps in IBD: Iron, B12 and More

Guidelines recommend screening everyone with IBD for malnutrition and deficiencies [37]. Iron deficiency anaemia is especially common [38] and needs proper testing and treatment, sometimes with intravenous iron [39].

Vitamin B12 deficiency is a particular risk with ileal Crohn’s disease or bowel resection [40]. Food can support recovery; see iron-rich Indian foods and zinc-rich foods, but do not self-supplement without testing.

Probiotics, FMT and Curcumin: Hype or Help?

Gut bacteria make short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate that help regulate the gut lining and immune response [41], which is why microbiome-based ideas are popular. A multi-strain probiotic helped induce remission in mild to moderate ulcerative colitis in an Indian trial [42].

Intensive faecal microbiota transplantation worked better than placebo in active ulcerative colitis, but it remains a specialist, trial-based treatment [43]. Curcumin added to standard medicine helped maintain remission in one small Japanese trial [44]. These are add-ons, not replacements. To choose a supplement safely, start with how to choose the best probiotics and prebiotics and probiotics.

Stress, Sleep and the Gut-Brain Axis

Stress does not cause IBD, but the gut and brain talk constantly, and that conversation can shape symptoms [45]. Psychological therapies may improve distress and quality of life, although evidence that they change inflammation itself is limited [46]. Explore the gut-brain connection and the vagus nerve.

IBD in Teens and Young Athletes

IBD often begins in the teens and twenties, when growth, school, sport and exams all compete for energy. Regular physical activity was linked with a lower risk of Crohn’s disease [47], and exercise was associated with fewer flares in people in remission [48].

In children, guidelines stress monitoring growth and using nutrition therapy as part of Crohn’s treatment [49] and in colitis care [50]. Young athletes need enough fuel and protein to train and heal, which is where individual sports nutrition and child and teen nutrition planning matters.

How a Gut Health Nutritionist Supports IBD Care

I work alongside your gastroenterologist. My role is to review your diet quality and nutrient gaps, build a plan around Indian food habits, guide safe reintroduction after restriction, check supplements for safety and help you eat well in both flare and remission. If you want support, explore my gut health nutrition service or contact me.

IBD FAQs

  1. Is IBD the same as IBS?

No. IBD involves visible, measurable inflammation of the gut. IBS is a functional disorder without that damage, though the two can overlap [19].

  1. Can IBD be cured?

There is no medical cure for Crohn’s disease, but many people reach long remission. Ulcerative colitis can be cured by removing the colon, which is a major decision made with your surgeon [22] [23].

  1. Is IBD an autoimmune disease?

IBD is an immune-mediated inflammatory condition. Doctors often avoid calling it purely autoimmune because gut bacteria and environment seem to drive the immune reaction too [12].

  1. Can stress cause IBD?

Stress is not thought to cause IBD, but it can influence symptoms through the gut-brain axis [45].

  1. What foods trigger IBD flares?

There is no universal list. Triggers differ between people, so a short, guided food and symptom diary works better than cutting out whole food groups [26].

  1. Can you exercise with IBD?

Usually yes, and regular activity appears helpful during remission. Adjust intensity during flares and talk to your care team [48].

  1. Can IBD cause weight loss and anaemia?

Yes. Poor absorption, reduced appetite, blood loss and inflammation can all contribute, which is why nutrient testing matters [37] [38].

This article is educational and does not replace medical care. If you have blood in your stool, persistent diarrhoea, unexplained weight loss or severe pain, see a doctor promptly.

High Fibre Foods for Piles (Haemorrhoids): What to Eat, What to Limit

Nobody brings up piles in social conversations, yet they are one of the most common reasons people end up in a doctor’s clinic with a very red face. In a US survey, about 4% of adults reported symptomatic haemorrhoids [1], while a screening colonoscopy study in Austria found haemorrhoids in almost 39% of adults examined [2]. Many people have them and few talk about it.

The good news: for most mild to moderate piles, what you eat is one of the most useful tools you have. This guide shows which high fibre foods help, how to add them without bloating, and when piles are not the whole story. If you want the fibre basics first, start with my guide to dietary fibre.

What Are Piles (Haemorrhoids)?

Piles are swollen, inflamed cushions of blood vessels and tissue in the anal canal. Everyone has these cushions as normal anatomy [5]; they become “piles” when they enlarge and cause symptoms [3]. Internal piles sit inside the canal and usually cause painless bright red bleeding or a feeling of fullness. External piles sit under the skin around the anus and can be itchy, sore or swollen.

Straining, long-standing constipation, hard stools and sitting on the toilet for long periods are all linked to piles [4] [6]. That is why diet, which controls stool texture, comes first.

Why High Fibre Foods Help Piles

Fibre adds bulk and holds water in the stool, making it softer and easier to pass without straining. A review of trials found that fibre cut the risk of persistent symptoms and bleeding in people with haemorrhoids by roughly half [7] [8], with the clearest benefit seen for bleeding and overall symptoms.

In an older double-blind trial, a high-fibre supplement reduced both bleeding and pain [9], and psyllium reduced bleeding from internal piles in another [10]. Surgical guidelines place fibre and fluids first for piles of every grade [11].

Clinical insight: For most people, piles are a stool texture problem long before they are a surgical problem. Fixing the stool is the first, cheapest and safest step.

One caution: fibre is not a cure-all for constipation. Specialists note that it helps many people but not everyone [12] [15]. It increased stool frequency in constipated people overall [13], yet in a small study of people with chronic constipation, cutting fibre back eased bloating and improved bowel frequency [14]. If more fibre makes you worse, read why “eat more fibre” doesn’t always work and why am I always constipated.

Which Type of Fibre Is Best for Piles?

Both types matter, but not equally:

  • Soluble fibre (oats, psyllium or isabgol, dals, beans, guava, apple, flaxseed, chia) forms a soft gel that holds water and softens stool. Psyllium is among the best-studied fibre supplements for stool softening [17].

  • Insoluble fibre (whole wheat, bran, vegetable skins) adds bulk. Among fibres, cereal fibre, especially wheat bran, raised stool weight the most in a review of trials [16].

If you also have IBS, favour soluble fibre. In IBS, soluble fibre helped while bran did not and may worsen symptoms [18] [19]. My posts on stomach pain after every meal and bloating cover this overlap.

How Much Fibre and Water Do You Need?

Aim for at least 25 to 30 g of fibre a day as an adult [20] [21], which is roughly 14 g per 1,000 kcal [22]. Most people eat far less, so build up gradually, adding a few grams every week.

Fibre without fluid can backfire. Extra water made a high-fibre diet work better in people with constipation [23], although evidence that water alone cures constipation is limited [24]. A practical rule is pale-yellow urine throughout the day.

Oats and dals. Oats are not only about stool: their beta-glucan also lowers LDL cholesterol [25], and pulses supply fibre, protein and micronutrients together [26]. Try my easy lentil recipes.

Prunes, figs and kiwi. Dried plums (prunes) improved stool frequency and consistency, and did at least as well as psyllium in one trial [27] [28]. In another trial, green kiwifruit, psyllium and prunes each improved bowel function in chronic constipation [29]. A fig (anjeer) paste also helped functional constipation in a placebo-controlled trial [30]. Soaked anjeer is a very Indian way to use that.

Seeds and isabgol. Flaxseed or psyllium improved constipation in a randomised trial in people with type 2 diabetes [31]. See flaxseed benefits and chia seeds. Take isabgol with a full glass of water, and check with your doctor if you take regular medicines, since fibre can affect how some are absorbed.

Curd and buttermilk. Probiotics modestly improved stool frequency and transit time in a meta-analysis [32]. Read curd vs probiotic yogurt and buttermilk benefits.

Whole grains. Swap refined flour and polished rice for whole-wheat atta, millets, brown or wild rice and jackfruit flour roti.

A piles-friendly day on a plate

Breakfast: oats porridge with a spoon of ground flaxseed and a pear. Lunch: two whole-wheat rotis, a bowl of dal, a vegetable sabzi and a salad. Snack: a guava or soaked anjeer. Dinner: vegetable khichdi with millets and a glass of buttermilk. That adds up to roughly 30 to 35 g of fibre, with water through the day.

What to Limit With Piles

  • Refined, low-fibre foods such as white bread, biscuits, bakery items and fast food, which make stools smaller and harder.

  • Skipping water while eating more fibre.

  • Straining and phone-scrolling on the toilet. Sitting for long periods and pushing is the exact thing piles dislike.

Some people notice flare-ups with alcohol, very spicy meals or a lot of coffee. A French study linked such dietary habits with haemorrhoidal symptoms [33], and coffee does stimulate the colon, including decaffeinated coffee [34]. The evidence is limited, so keep a short symptom diary instead of banning foods you enjoy.

Toilet Habits That Protect Your Piles

Indian toilets were ahead of their time. A squatting posture reduced straining and the time taken to pass stool compared with sitting [35], and a device that raised the feet to mimic squatting improved the sense of complete evacuation in healthy people [36]. If you use a western toilet, put your feet on a low stool, lean forward and do not wait around for more than a few minutes.

Piles in Pregnancy and After Delivery

Piles are common in late pregnancy and after childbirth, along with fissures [37] [39]. Dietary fibre and fluids are the first-line, safe starting point, although the trial evidence in pregnancy is limited [38]. Check with your obstetrician before using any supplement or medicine. More in my women’s health section.

Teens and Young Athletes

True piles are less common in teenagers, and constipation is the more usual culprit: roughly one in ten children has functional constipation [41]. A simple fibre target for children is their age plus 5 g a day [40]. Young athletes on low-fibre, high-protein diets often fall short, so I build fibre and fluids into their plans through my sports nutrition and child and teen nutrition services.

Is It Piles or Something Else?

SymptomOften points toWhat to do
Bright red blood on paper, painlessInternal pilesFibre, fluids, see a doctor to confirm
Sharp pain during and after stool, small blood streakAnal fissureFibre and see a doctor; bran helped prevent recurrence in one study [42], and fibre is first-line in guidelines [43]
Blood mixed in the stool, change in bowel habit, weight loss, anaemiaNeeds investigationSee a doctor promptly

Do not assume rectal bleeding is “just piles”. Blood mixed with stool and a change in bowel habit raised the likelihood of colorectal cancer in a systematic review [44]. Early-onset colorectal cancer is rising [46], and rectal bleeding, abdominal pain, diarrhoea and iron-deficiency anaemia are the key red flags in younger adults [45].

Bloody diarrhoea can also point to ulcerative colitis, a form of inflammatory bowel disease [47]. See a doctor if bleeding is new, repeated, heavy or you are over 40 or have a family history of bowel cancer.

Other Treatments Your Doctor May Suggest

Diet works alongside medical care, not instead of it. Doctors may recommend flavonoid medicines, which reduced bleeding and other symptoms in trials though the quality of evidence is limited [48]. Warm sitz baths are widely used for comfort, even though firm evidence is thin [49].

For larger or persistent piles, procedures such as rubber band ligation may be needed, which causes less pain than surgery but a higher chance of recurrence [50]. I explain how a nutritionist and doctor work together in gut health nutritionist vs gastroenterologist.

How to Add Fibre Without Bloating

  1. Add one new fibre food every few days.

  2. Soak and well-cook dals and beans.

  3. Drink water with every fibre-rich meal.

  4. Move daily; walking helps the gut move too.

  5. If gas or bloating persists, ask a gut health nutritionist to tailor your fibre types. Explore prebiotics and probiotics and the top 10 foods for gut health.

FAQs: High Fibre Foods for Piles

  1. Can piles go away with diet alone?

Mild piles often settle with higher fibre, more fluid and better toilet habits [7]. Larger or persistent piles may need treatment.

  1. What is the best fruit for piles?

Guava, pear and apple with skin, prunes and figs are good choices for fibre and softer stools [27] [30].

  1. Is isabgol good for piles?

Psyllium reduced bleeding in trials, so it is a reasonable option with plenty of water [10].

  1. Should I avoid spicy food with piles?

It bothers some people and not others. The evidence is limited, so track your own pattern [33].

  1. How much fibre should I eat for piles?

Aim for at least 25 to 30 g a day, increasing gradually [20].

  1. Can too much fibre make piles worse?

A sudden jump or too little water can worsen bloating and hard stools, and some people with chronic constipation do better with less [14].

  1. When should I see a doctor?

For any new, repeated or heavy rectal bleeding, blood mixed with stool, a change in bowel habit, weight loss or anaemia [44] [45].

Get Personalised Help

If piles, constipation or bloating keep coming back, the fix is rarely “just eat more fibre”. It is the right fibre, in the right amount, with the right habits for your gut. Explore my gut health nutrition service or contact me.

This article is educational and does not replace medical care. Never ignore rectal bleeding: have it checked by a doctor.
